meta.regime: The debasement trade is intact but its plumbing changed overnight. Until yesterday the dollar short and the gold long were the same position - two expressions of one loss of confidence in US fiscal credibility. Monday broke that: Bessent's Iran sanctions escalation gave the DOLLAR a safe-haven bid, DXY reclaiming 99.00 for the first time since last Wednesday's plunge, while gold ALSO rose to 4,643.52. When gold and the dollar rally together on the same headline, the geopolitical premium is being paid in both, and the two trades have to be sized separately. Gold keeps the geopolitics and the debasement; the dollar short is now a pure Fed trade that has to survive a +0.3% core PCE forecast on Wednesday and Warsh on Friday. The second break is in energy: crude did NOT respond to the escalation - WTI 84.94, Brent 92.02, both marginally lower - while European and Asian gas ripped. The war premium has migrated from oil to gas, which supports the euro's inflation story and removes the loonie's last leg.

September hike odds have collapsed to roughly 31% from 82% in mid-July, so the risk is now a HAWKISH surprise into a market that has stopped pricing one. Core PCE (forecast +0.3% m/m) lands Wednesday Aug 26 at 12:30Z; Australia's July CPI indicator, expected to cool hard to 3.2% from 3.8%, lands eleven hours earlier at 01:30Z.

dailyRead: Start with the correction to yesterday, because it changes the sizing of the two biggest positions on the book. Monday's file said gold and the short dollar were the same fiscal-credibility trade and should be held as one position. Monday's tape falsified that. Treasury Secretary Bessent unveiled Operation Economic Outcast on Monday afternoon - a zero-leakage crackdown on Iranian oil smuggling and sanctions evasion, with the Treasury sanctioning close to sixty entities, individuals and vessels across shipping, oil, crypto, gold and aviation, and secondary sanctions threatened on a country-by-country timeline rather than immediately. Notably no penalties were named against China, the largest buyer of Iranian crude, and Bessent declined to say which countries would be targeted. Iran answered in kind: ships violating transit rules face detention or confiscation, security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to halt oil flow out of Hormuz if any neighbour joins the economic crackdown, the Iranian parliament is advancing a plan for Hormuz service fees, and Oman's foreign minister Badr al-Busaidi travels to Tehran today. On that headline the DOLLAR caught a safe-haven bid, DXY reclaiming 99.00 for the first time since last Wednesday's plunge and closing 98.889, up 0.09% - and gold rose at the same time, to 4,643.52, having traded just shy of 4,650. Two assets that were supposed to be opposite legs of one trade went up together. Practically: gold now owns the geopolitical premium AND the debasement premium, which makes XAU the cleanest expression on the page and keeps it at HIGH conviction. The dollar short loses its geopolitical hedge and becomes a pure Fed trade, which is why DXY comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM, because that Fed trade has to survive a core PCE print forecast to ACCELERATE to 0.3% month-on-month on Wednesday and Kevin Warsh's first keynote as Chair on Friday. And understand the asymmetry properly: September hike odds have fallen to roughly 31% from 82% in mid-July, so the market has now largely stopped pricing the hawkish outcome the three FOMC dissenters are still arguing for. A hawkish Warsh is no longer the consensus tail - it is the un-priced one. The second and more surprising thing is what crude did NOT do. On the single largest sanctions escalation of this war, WTI closed at 84.94, down 0.08%, and Brent at 92.017, down 0.17%. A market that refuses to rally on unambiguously bullish supply news is telling you the physical premium is exhausted, and it fits with Iran quietly granting Iraqi tankers passage and with the flow data showing roughly 130 transits a day. So USOIL comes off a MEDIUM long to RANGE - not short, because Rezaei's threat and the transit-fee bill are live tail risks, but no longer long. Where the premium DID go is gas: UK gas rose 3.49% on the day and 10.90% on the week, German gas 3.61% and 10.63%, EU TTF is up 7.37% weekly and 17.15% on the month, and Asian LNG 8.77% weekly. That distinction matters because it keeps Lagarde's energy channel wide open - euro-area energy HICP is already 10.0% - while removing the last support under the Canadian dollar. Third change, and the one that reopens a trade: copper. At 6.5966 dollars a pound it is now UP 1.76% on the week, against Monday's file which had it down 0.87% and called it the warning light on every Aussie long. That light is off. Copper is still the laggard of the metals complex - gold +7.12%, silver +7.71%, platinum +7.77% on the week against copper's +1.76% - so the industrial cycle is convalescing rather than accelerating, and XCU stays RANGE. But the divergence that was the bearish tell has closed. On top of that the RBA minutes at 01:30Z read hawkish: the Board considered raising the cash rate pre-emptively against the risk that the Middle East conflict drags on or the AI boom proves larger than anticipated, several members judged it quite possible that upside inflation risks crystallise, and the Board agreed it stands ready to raise if they do. Against that the same minutes concede inflation came in lower than forecast and the jobs market is softening faster than expected, and the July labour break is still unrepaired - employment minus 15,827, unemployment 4.5% and a post-COVID high, participation down to 66.9%. Consensus for Wednesday's July CPI indicator is a sharp cooling to 3.2% from 3.8%. So Australia stays at 0, but it is a genuinely two-sided 0 now rather than a deteriorating one, and the AUD shorts come down in size: EUR/AUD from HIGH to MEDIUM, GBP/AUD from MEDIUM to LOW-MED. Canada was the day's actual loser. USD/CAD rose 0.49% to 1.38265 and the loonie was the weakest major on the board at minus 0.57% against the dollar. Yesterday's downgrade to 0 was the right call and today's price action confirms it: oil was the only leg and oil did not respond even to an escalation. The domestic data is unchanged and poor - retail sales minus 0.8% month-on-month, composite PMI 49.7 and services 49.1 both contracting, annual GDP minus 0.1% with the quarterly rate at 0.0%, terms of trade 101, house prices minus 2.3% year-on-year - offset by July CPI at 3.0%, the ceiling of the control range, energy inflation 16.6%, producer prices plus 12.4%, employment plus 75,100 and unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%. One small positive worth naming before Friday: TE has monthly GDP at plus 0.2% in June. Canada holds 0 but it is the weakest of the zeros, and Friday's GDP at 12:30Z is what takes it to negative. USD/CAD accordingly goes from a MEDIUM short to RANGE - the trade is now losing on both legs. Japan holds +1 and the thesis is unchanged but the tape is uncomfortable. USD/JPY closed at 159.071, up 0.05%, grinding north of 159 on the same haven bid, and Bloomberg is already framing it as the Bank facing pressure with the yen near 160 while September hike bets surge. The fundamentals are the best on the board: Polymarket at 84% for a 25bp move to 1.25% on September 17-18, Reuters reporting the Bank is considering a faster pace than roughly twice a year, PM Takaichi now supporting hikes, July CPI 1.9% with core 1.8% and core-core 1.9%, Tokyo core 1.9%, wage growth 3.4% with real earnings positive a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, machinery orders plus 16.9% year-on-year. Deputy Governor Himino speaks before the decision and Ueda is expected to brief after a G20 gathering in the US. Keep USD/JPY a HIGH-conviction short and treat 160 as the defined invalidation - and note that at 160 the Ministry of Finance has already intervened once, so above the line the MoF and the BoJ are both on your side of the trade. Europe holds +2 and stays the strongest currency. EUR/USD is 1.16755, up 0.82% on the week and 2.71% on the month. The gas move helps the hawkish case directly: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3% and energy 10.0%, national prints hotter still at Germany 2.8%, Spain 3.6%, France 2.1%, and TE's model still carrying 2.65% refi by quarter-end which is the September 10 hike. Depo re-verified at 2.25%. The dovish counterweight is unchanged and real - TE's ECB page leads with a wait-and-see characterisation, negotiated wage growth slowed to 2.44% and consumer inflation expectations fell a third month to 2.9%. Today's German Ifo at 08:00Z, expected to improve to 87.2 from 86.6, and Thursday's meeting accounts at 09:30Z are the two tests. Sterling holds +1 on the 3.75% Bank Rate, the 6-3 vote and the G10's highest gilt near 5.1%, with July CPI 2.9% but core FLAT at 2.6%, services cooled to 3.4% and wages down to 4.1% - and UK gas up 10.90% on the week and electricity 4.55% points straight at another October Ofgem uplift, which is the one thing that could rescue the three dissenters. Cable 1.36443. New Zealand holds +1 and was quietly the best major on the week at plus 1.20%, absorbing a soft June retail sales print at minus 0.5% and a record July import bill that took the trade balance to minus 1,949 million New Zealand dollars. TE's model still forecasts an OCR of 2.75% on September 2, but the July statement only called further increases possible and cited the partial Hormuz reopening easing price pressure, and two-year inflation expectations fell to 2.34%. Treat September 2 as genuinely two-way. Switzerland holds +1: USD/CHF at 0.80124 is flat on the day and down 1.18% on the week, on Q2 GDP at plus 1.5% quarter-on-quarter, a record July trade surplus of 8,141 million francs, a services PMI of 63.9 and ZEW at plus 10 - with the policy rate at 0% and SNB reserves at 768,260 million francs after rising 9.4 billion in July, which keeps Schlegel's intervention warning as the named invalidator. The instruction for the day: run gold at full size, run the yen and franc shorts against the dollar, cut the DXY and USD/CAD expressions, take crude off, and keep the Aussie book small until 01:30Z Wednesday.

USD.when: Sept 16-17 FOMC (hold - and September hike odds have fallen to ~31% from 82% in mid-July)
USD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE this morning at 3.75% upper bound (3.50-3.75%), held Jul 29 in a 9-3 vote with three presidents dissenting for a quarter-point hike - the widest split in roughly two decades. TE macro re-verified and unchanged: CPI 3.4% from 3.5% and a five-month low, core 2.5% from 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%, unemployment 4.1% from 4.2%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000, average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m, job vacancies down to 7,140k from 7,500k, August flash composite PMI 56.0 with services 56.8 and manufacturing 53.2, consumer confidence 51.0 from 55.2, retail sales -0.6% m/m. Two things changed overnight and both cut the same way. First, the dollar caught a SAFE-HAVEN bid on Bessent's Iran escalation, DXY reclaiming 99.00 for the first time since last Wednesday and closing 98.889 - and gold rose at the same time. The dollar short has therefore lost its geopolitical hedge: DXY and XAU are no longer one position, and DXY drops from HIGH to MEDIUM conviction. Second, and more important for the week, the market has now largely stopped pricing the hawkish outcome. September hike odds are roughly 31%, down from 82% in mid-July, with futures oscillating in a 35-65% band on some measures. That means a hawkish Warsh is the UN-PRICED tail rather than the consensus one - the opposite of how Monday's file framed it. The week's structure: Tuesday Aug 25 at 14:00Z brings Conference Board consumer confidence and new home sales, with the Richmond Fed survey and a 2-year auction alongside. Wednesday Aug 26 at 12:30Z brings core PCE, forecast to ACCELERATE to 0.3% m/m, against a Q2 GDP second estimate expected LOWER - a hot-inflation, slowing-growth pairing that is awkward for a committee with three hawkish dissenters. Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote, expected around 10:00 ET; the official topic is financial innovation in payments, he has moved away from heavy forward guidance and described the remarks as a blank piece of paper. Fiscal backdrop worth naming: the July federal deficit was 432.3 billion dollars, the largest monthly shortfall since March 2021, taking the fiscal-year total to 1.8 trillion with two months still to run. That is the engine under gold. Hold USD at -2, cut size on every dollar-leg expression.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z (TE model still 2.65% refi by quarter-end; the gas move reinforces the hawkish case)
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE this morning at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, with main refinancing at 2.40% and marginal lending at 2.65%. Use the 2.25% depo, never the 2.40% headline. The single most useful development for the euro overnight is where the war premium went. Crude did not move - WTI 84.94, Brent 92.017 - but GAS did: EU TTF is 68.33 EUR/MWh and up 7.37% on the week and 17.15% on the month, German gas 68.96 and up 3.61% today with 10.63% weekly, UK gas +3.49% today and +10.90% weekly, Asian LNG +8.77% weekly, German electricity +24.43% on the month. Gas, not crude, is the euro-area inflation channel, and it is running hot into a September decision. The price data supports it: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services 3.3% from 3.2%, energy HICP 10.0% from 8.5%, and the national prints hotter still with Germany 2.8% from 2.3%, Spain 3.6% from 3.2%, France 2.1% from 1.8% and Italy 2.9%. Activity is improving: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, August composite PMI 52.1 and a nine-month high, manufacturing 52.8 and a four-year high, services 51.7, ZEW 31.4 from 23.4, unemployment stable at 6.3%, employment +0.1% q/q. TE's model still puts the policy rate at 2.65% refi by the end of this quarter, which is the September 10 move. The honest counterweight is unchanged: TE's ECB summary leads with the July 23 hold and a more CAUTIOUS, wait-and-see tone because softer inflation, wage growth, activity and expectations have reduced the urgency, and the supporting evidence is real - negotiated wage growth slowed to 2.44% in Q2 from 2.56%, consumer inflation expectations fell a third month to 2.9%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y, food inflation only 0.8%, retail sales -0.3% m/m. EUR holds +2 and stays the strongest currency on the board. Two tests today and Thursday: German Ifo at 08:00Z, expected 87.2 from 86.6, and the July meeting accounts Thursday Aug 27 at 09:30Z. EUR/USD 1.16755, +0.82% on the week.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; the gas spike is the dissenters' only remaining argument)
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%, held Jul 30 but 6-3 with a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. Both decisive prints have landed and both cut dovish once you look past the headline. Labour: wage growth eased to 4.1% including bonuses from 4.4%, employment change fell to +83,000 from +147,000, unemployment held at 4.9% against expectations of a fall to 4.8%, and the claimant count FELL 11,000. Prices: July CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first increase since March, but the driver was administered energy on the Ofgem cap adjustment - core CPI held FLAT at 2.6% and services inflation COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. Activity is decent but decelerating: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q from +0.6%, annual rate 1.2%, August composite PMI 52.5. What changed overnight is the energy channel, and it works in sterling's favour for the wrong reason: UK gas rose 3.49% on the day to 169.17 GBp/thm and is up 10.90% on the week and 19.08% on the month, with UK electricity +1.56% today and +4.55% weekly. That points at another administered-energy uplift in October, which would re-accelerate headline CPI and hand the three dissenters the evidence they are currently losing. Sterling is holding on yield rather than policy - the 10-year gilt near 5.1% is still the G10's highest - and there is no UK data on today's slate. GBP holds +1. Express it against the dollar, the Aussie and the loonie; not against the euro, the franc or the yen. Cable 1.36443, +0.74% on the week.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (84% priced on Polymarket; Reuters says the BoJ wants a FASTER pace than twice a year)
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE this morning at 1.00%, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY holds +1. The fundamental case is the strongest on the board and it strengthened again overnight, but the tape is uncomfortable and traders should know which is which. On fundamentals: Polymarket assigns 84% to a 25bp increase at the September 17-18 meeting against 15% for no change, Reuters reports on sources that the Bank is eyeing a hike as soon as September AND considering a faster pace than its current roughly twice a year, citing Middle East price pressure, strong global AI demand and the yen's downtrend, and Prime Minister Takaichi - who once called it stupid for the Bank to consider increases - now supports them. TE re-verified: July national CPI 1.9% from 1.6% and the highest since December 2025, core 1.8% from 1.6%, core-core 1.9% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% and Tokyo headline 2.0%, services 1.2%, goods 2.7%, food 3.5%, PPI 7.2%, inflation expectations 2.7%. Domestic conditions are the best in three decades: labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, real earnings +1.6% and positive a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, industrial output +4.9% y/y, machinery orders +16.9% y/y and +9.7% m/m, August Reuters Tankan 18 from 13, manufacturing PMI 55.1, services 52.3, composite 53.4. On the tape: USD/JPY closed 159.071, UP 0.05%, grinding higher on the same haven bid that lifted the dollar, and Bloomberg is framing it as the Bank facing pressure with the yen near 160 while September bets surge. The external account still caps the score - a record import price index of 200, import prices +29.1% y/y, terms of trade 81.62 and a July trade balance of MINUS JPY 634bn - and today's flat crude does not repair it the way Monday's selloff promised. Treat 160 as the defined invalidation on any yen long, and note the asymmetry: above 160 the Ministry of Finance has already intervened once, so both the MoF and a tightening BoJ sit on your side. Deputy Governor Himino speaks before the decision and Ueda is expected to brief after a G20 gathering in the US. Tokyo August CPI and July unemployment land Thursday Aug 27 at 23:30Z.

AUD.when: Sept 29 (hold - but the minutes show the Board debated a HIKE, and Wednesday's CPI decides it)
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, held unanimously on Aug 11. The August minutes released this morning at 01:30Z are more hawkish than the market expected and they change the shape of the Australian risk without changing the score. The Board considered raising the cash rate pre-emptively to guard against a rise in inflation if the Middle East conflict drags on or the AI boom proves larger than anticipated; it also flagged risks from slower productivity growth, higher pass-through of business costs and a more resilient domestic economy. Several members judged it quite possible that the upside risks crystallise, while others saw offsetting downside risks, so there was some time to assess incoming data - and the Board agreed it stands ready to raise if the upside risks materialise. Against that the same minutes concede inflation came in lower than forecast and the jobs market is softening faster than expected, and the Board agreed the current rate appears to be working to bring the economy into balance. The hard data is still the problem: July employment FELL 15,827 against consensus of +20-25k, full-time +16,333 but part-time -32,160, unemployment 4.5% and a post-COVID high, participation 66.9%, employment-to-population 63.9%, job vacancies 330,000, terms of trade 112 from 117, business confidence -6, current account a record -AUD 27.1bn, wage growth only 3.2%. What keeps AUD at 0 rather than negative is price and carry: 4.35% is the G10's highest cash rate, Q2 weighted median CPI ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, trimmed mean 3.6%, services 4.0%, headline 3.8%, consumer inflation expectations rose again to 4.9% in August, consumer confidence jumped to 88.9 from 83.9, August PMIs expansionary at 52.5 composite. The copper picture has flipped: at 6.5966 USD/lb it is UP 1.76% on the week against Monday's -0.87%, so the industrial warning light on every Aussie long is off - though copper still badly lags gold +7.12%, silver +7.71% and platinum +7.77%, so call it convalescence not acceleration. AUD/USD 0.71682, +0.89% on the week and +7.43% YTD, but it was the day's laggard on risk aversion. The July CPI indicator lands Wednesday Aug 26 at 01:30Z and consensus is a sharp cooling to 3.2% from 3.8% - a genuine binary. AUD holds 0; cut the size on every AUD short until that print.

NZD.when: Sept 2, 02:00Z (TE model 2.75% - but treat it as genuinely open, not a done deal)
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.50% after the 25bp hike on Jul 8, the first in three years. NZD holds +1 and was quietly the best major on the week at +1.20%, which is the notable thing given what it absorbed: June retail sales fell 0.5% m/m against +1.0%, and the July trade balance printed MINUS NZD 1,949 million against -237 million, on a record import bill of 9,340 million and exports down to 7,391 million - the largest gap in nearly two years. The kiwi held multi-month highs through all of it. Keep the franc long against the dollar, the Aussie and the loonie; keep it flat against the other +1 currencies. Treat SNB intervention as the named invalidator on every CHF position, and remember some of the Q2 GDP strength is pharma front-running of US tariffs and will not repeat.

catalysts.note: The event of the month, expected ~10:00 ET. No policy record, no forward guidance, described by Warsh as a blank piece of paper. Crucially, September hike odds have fallen to ~31% from 82% in mid-July, so a hawkish tone is now the UN-priced tail. Carry reduced size.

TE's model forecasts 2.75% but the July statement only calls further hikes POSSIBLE and projects inflation falling from a 3.9% peak. Two-year expectations fell to 2.34%. Genuinely two-way, and the whole NZD story.

Hold at 2.25% expected for a seventh straight meeting. With the composite PMI at 49.7, services at 49.1 and crude refusing to rally even on an Iran escalation, the BoC has no reason to move and CAD has no rate support.

TE's model still implies a 25bp hike of the deposit facility to 2.50%, and the gas spike supports it, but the ECB's own communication has turned more cautious. The single biggest event for the euro's +2 score.

84% priced on Polymarket for 25bp to 1.25%, with Reuters reporting the Bank is considering a faster pace than twice a year. Deputy Governor Himino speaks and Ueda briefs after a G20 gathering beforehand. No fixed release time - the statement lands in the Tokyo morning.

catalysts.event: Iran sanctions / Strait of Hormuz escalation watch
catalysts.note: Direction reversed: Bessent's Operation Economic Outcast sanctioned ~60 entities across shipping, oil, crypto, gold and aviation with secondary sanctions on a country timeline. Iran threatens seizures, parliament advances transit fees, Rezaei threatens to halt flows. Oman's FM is in Tehran today. Note crude did NOT rally - the premium is in gas and gold.

Reserves ROSE to CHF 768,260m in July from 758,851m and Schlegel keeps reaffirming increased readiness to intervene against rapid or one-way franc appreciation. The named invalidator on every CHF long.

USD/JPY at 159.071 is grinding back toward the 160 line where the Ministry has already acted. Above 160 intervention risk works FOR a yen long, since the MoF and a tightening BoJ would be pushing the same way.

geopolitics: The direction of the Iran story reversed again, and this time the FX transmission is the interesting part rather than the headline. On Monday afternoon Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled Operation Economic Outcast, billed as an economic D-Day: a zero-leakage crackdown on Iranian oil smuggling and sanctions evasion, with the Treasury designating close to sixty entities, individuals and vessels across shipping, oil, crypto, gold and aviation, plus illicit procurement of nuclear and missile technology. Bessent said there would be no minimal breathing space for the regime. Importantly the toughest blow was delayed: secondary sanctions will not be imposed immediately, each country instead gets a timeline to wind down Iran-related activity, no penalties were named against China - the largest buyer of Iranian crude - and Bessent declined to say which countries would be targeted first. Tehran answered on the water. Ships violating transit rules face detention or confiscation, top security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to halt oil flow out of the Strait of Hormuz altogether should any neighbouring country join the US crackdown, and the Iranian parliament is advancing a plan to levy service fees on Hormuz transits - a de facto toll on the world's most important chokepoint. At the same time Iran granted a number of Iraqi tankers passage, traffic remains reduced but functioning at roughly 130 transits a day, and Oman's foreign minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi arrives in Tehran today to discuss the strait. So the picture is escalation on the financial front and grinding, negotiated ambiguity on the physical one. The FX read follows from one observation: CRUDE DID NOT RALLY. WTI closed at 84.94, down 0.08%, and Brent at 92.017, down 0.17%, on the largest sanctions escalation of this war. That is the single most informative price on the page. The oil risk premium is exhausted at these levels, which is why USOIL comes off a long to a range and why the Canadian dollar - which has no other engine - was the weakest major of the session at minus 0.57%. Where the premium DID go is threefold. Into gas: UK gas rose 3.49% on the day and 10.90% on the week, German gas 3.61% and 10.63%, EU TTF is up 7.37% weekly and 17.15% monthly, Asian LNG 8.77% weekly, German electricity 24.43% on the month - which keeps the euro-area energy channel wide open behind EUR at +2 and squeezes German industry behind GER40. Into gold, which rose to 4,643.52 and traded just shy of 4,650. And, for the first time in this episode, into the DOLLAR, which reclaimed 99.00 on the index for the first time since last Wednesday. That last leg is the change that matters for positioning: when the dollar and gold rally on the same geopolitical headline they are no longer opposite sides of one trade, and the short-dollar and long-gold expressions have to be sized independently from today. Trade it as an escalating financial conflict layered on a stalemated physical one, with fat tails on both sides: a Rezaei-style closure attempt or a transit-fee regime would finally move crude, while a Muscat breakthrough takes gas back down and the euro with it.
